content:
Naval just said pure software is "rapidly becoming un-investable."

He's right. And most founders haven't felt it yet — but they will.

---

The moat you built on proprietary code? AI is dissolving it in real time.

What took a team of 10 engineers 6 months to build, a well-prompted model now scaffolds in weeks.

Code is no longer the defensible layer.

---

So what is?

- Data you own that others can't replicate
- Distribution built on trust and community
- Hardware integration that creates switching costs
- A model fine-tuned on proprietary signal

If your pitch is "we built it better" — that's not a moat anymore.

---

The paradox: engineers have never been more leveraged as individuals.

But engineering as a business category is getting compressed.

One amplifies human output. The other is a commoditized cost center.

Know which side of that line your company sits on.

---

If you're raising or building right now, your board WILL ask this question:

"Why can't a well-funded competitor replicate your core product with AI in 90 days?"

You need a real answer. Not a feature list.

---

What's your actual moat in an AI-commoditized world — data, distribution, hardware, or something else?

Drop it below. I'll tell you if I believe it.
source_story_title: Naval: Pure Software is 'Rapidly Becoming Un-Investable'
source_story_summary: Naval Ravikant posted a blunt, high-engagement claim that pure software businesses are rapidly becoming un-investable, a stark signal about how AI commoditization is eroding the defensibility of traditional software moats. A companion post elaborated that software engineers remain highly leveraged individuals — but framed within an AI-augmented world where the nature of value creation is shifting fundamentally.

content:
Saylor doesn't post for engagement. He posts to move conviction.
---
'The Turn of the Century' isn't a price call. It's a frame. He's not telling you to buy BTC. He's telling you what century you're operating in.
---
That framing matters more than any target. Institutions don't allocate to assets. They allocate to narratives with staying power. Saylor is manufacturing staying power in real time.
---
16k likes on a philosophical post with no price chart attached. That's not hype. That's a room full of treasury decision-makers taking notes.
---
The operators paying attention aren't asking "is Bitcoin going up?" They're asking "do I want to be on the wrong side of this narrative in 10 years?"
---
Hot take: Saylor's real product isn't Bitcoin exposure. It's certainty in an uncertain macro environment. And certainty is the scarcest asset in any boardroom right now.
---
If you're building a company or managing a treasury — what's your framework for when the Bitcoin reserve asset narrative becomes impossible to ignore? What's the threshold?
source_story_title: Saylor Posts 'The Turn of the Century' — Likely Bitcoin Macro Signal
source_story_summary: Michael Saylor shared a post titled 'The Turn of the Century' with an attached media item, generating significant engagement (15,868 likes, 1,687 RTs). While the full content is not visible, Saylor's consistent messaging centers on Bitcoin as the defining monetary asset of the 21st century, and this framing suggests a macro or philosophical statement about Bitcoin's role at a historical inflection point.
